This template has been created to help developers of population-based Optimal Care Pathways (OCPs) develop a high-quality and evidence-based resource that is consistent with the library of existing pathways. The template mirrors the core content of the cancer-specific OCP template and provides space to add considerations for a particular population group relevant to the Principles for Optimal Cancer Care <hyperlink to be added> and each pathway step. It contains two types of content:

• core content that is standard across all OCPs and cannot be changed

• editable content that must be completed or adapted for your population group.

OCPs@canceraustralia.gov.au

• Follow these instructions when developing your OCP. If you have any questions, contact Cancer Australia at

• Keep content high level and scannable. Avoid lengthy narrative paragraphs.

• Review the Principles for Optimal Cancer Care <hyperlink to be added> when developing content to avoid duplication and identify where cross-referencing is appropriate.

sections.headingText: Types of content in this template
sections.headingPrinted: Types of content in this template
sections.content:
• Black text is core content that cannot be edited. This is standard content across all OCPs.

• Text [highlighted in yellow] indicates words to be added / adapted for this population group / OCP.

• Purple boxes indicate content requiring developer input specific to this population group / OCP. Instructions are provided in purple text.

• Key considerations tables contain brief statements summarising what optimal care looks like at each step of the cancer pathway. Follow the purple prompts to add population-specific considerations as new rows in these tables.

• Checklists are actionable items for health professionals at key decision points. Follow the purple prompts to add any population-specific actions as new rows in these lists.

• Supportive care sections: Each step includes supportive care considerations. Follow the purple prompts to add population-specific content.

• 'Find out more' boxes are curated links to guidelines and resources. These will appear on the digital hub with links from relevant sections. Follow the purple prompts to add any specific resources for this population group and include the associated hyperlink.

sections.headingText: What you can and cannot change
sections.headingPrinted: What you can and cannot change
sections.content:
• Numbered headings and subheadings cannot be changed or reordered. This ensures consistency across the OCP library and aids with digitisation.

• Additional third-level subheadings (i.e. non-numbered headings) can be added within sections. Consider additional sub-headings sparingly.

• Sections can be removed where content is not relevant to this population group.

If you identify content that you believe should be added as core information to the template (e.g. a new section, consideration or action relevant to all population-based OCPs), note this separately with Cancer Australia. Developers cannot edit core template content directly. Suggestions will be considered as part of the centralised review process.

Optimal Care Pathways (OCPs) are nationally endorsed evidence-and consensus-based guides to best practice care across the cancer continuum. They set a national standard for consistent, high-quality cancer care for everyone in Australia, regardless of who they are or where they live.

Australian Cancer Plan

National Optimal Care Pathways

Framework

OCPs are embedded within the as national standards for delivery of high-quality, consistent cancer care. Their development is guided by the , which provides a consistent approach to prioritisation, development, update and endorsement of OCPs and supports their adoption into health systems.

sections.headingText: Intent of the Optimal Care Pathways
sections.headingPrinted: Intent of the Optimal Care Pathways
sections.content:
Map nationally agreed best practice approaches to cancer care, placing the person with cancer at the centre of care.

Set the standard for quality cancer care in Australia by describing what optimal care looks like across the cancer continuum.

Reduce unwarranted variation in access, care and outcomes by providing a nationally consistent approach to benchmark and improve services and practice.

Guide service improvement by helping health services identify gaps and opportunities to achieve optimal care.

Support clinician practice by giving health professionals evidence-based information, checklists and tools to understand and deliver best practice care.

Inform and empower people affected by cancer to have informed conversations with their healthcare teams about optimal care and what they should expect.

Drive equity by promoting accessible, culturally safe and responsive care that reduces unwarranted variations in access, care and outcomes.

Cancer-specific OCPs

Provide guidance on prevention, early detection, diagnosis, treatment and care of specific cancer types, including recommended timeframes.

Population-based OCPs

Provide guidance on considerations across the cancer continuum for priority population groups who have distinct care needs.

Cancer-specific and population-based OCPs can be used separately or together to create a tailored pathway based on individual needs.

All OCPs are underpinned by Principles for Optimal Cancer Care. <hyperlink to be added>

OCPs are designed for use by all those involved in cancer care.

Health professionals

Health service administrators, managers and policy makers

People with cancer, their carers and families

OCPs are designed to be used with clinical guidelines and eviQ protocols as part of a comprehensive approach to cancer care.

Optimal Care Pathways Nationally endorsed cancer care pathways with standards of cancer care that everyone with cancer in Australia should expect

Clinical practice guidelines

Systematically developed evidence-based statements and recommendations to support decision-making in specific clinical circumstances

eviQ protocols

Evidence-based, consensus driven cancer treatment protocols to guide use of specific treatments or interventions at point of care

OCPs do not constitute medical advice or replace clinical judgement. They provide links to relevant guidelines, protocols and other resources.

Each OCP is available as a suite of three complementary resources, designed for different users and purposes:

Full OCP

OCP Quick Reference Guide

OCP Consumer Guide:

Guide to best practice cancer care

Comprehensive evidence-and consensus-based guide for health professionals and health services

Summary of the full OCP for use at point of care

Plain-language summary for people affected by cancer, their carers and families

Available in multiple languages

The Principles for Optimal Cancer Care set the foundations for delivery of information, care and support for everyone who is at risk of and affected by cancer. Everyone in the healthcare system is responsible for delivering cancer care aligned to the Principles.

Principles are relevant to all cancer types and all populations. Population-based OCPs may identify unique considerations for implementation for a particular population group.

Equity <Link to Principle > <hyperlink to be added>

1

Health equity in cancer outcomes is the absence of disparities for people with different levels of social advantage.

Person-centred care <Link to Principle > <hyperlink to be added>

2

Person-centred care means informing and involving people in their care, and respecting and responding to their individual needs, preferences and values, as well as those of their families and carers.

Safe and quality care <Link to Principle> <hyperlink to be added>

3

Safe and quality care means delivering the most appropriate and best-value care, while keeping people safe from preventable harm in the delivery of that care.

Multidisciplinary care <Link to Principle> <hyperlink to be added>

4

Multidisciplinary care is an integrated team approach that involves all relevant health professionals discussing all relevant treatment options and making joint recommendations about treatment and supportive care plans that consider the individual characteristics and preferences of the person with cancer.

Supportive care <Link to Principle> <hyperlink to be added>

5

Supportive care involves prevention and management of the adverse effects of cancer and its treatment, including management of physical and psychological symptoms and side effects across the cancer continuum. Supportive care aims to improve the quality of rehabilitation, secondary cancer prevention, survivorship, and end-of-life care.

Navigation and care coordination <Link to Principle> <hyperlink to be added>

6

Navigation and care coordination are related person-centred interventions that aim to empower patients, families and carers affected by cancer to facilitate safe and timely access to optimal cancer-related care and support.

Communication <Link to Principle> <hyperlink to be added>

7

Good communication is an essential part of cancer care and a responsibility of everyone involved in health care across the cancer continuum.

Research and clinical trials <Link to Principle> <hyperlink to be added>

8

Research and clinical trials generate evidence to improve understanding of cancer and to accelerate progress in prevention, detection, diagnosis, treatment, supportive care, survivorship care, palliative and end-of-life care.

sections.headingText: Steps of the Optimal Care Pathway
sections.headingPrinted: Steps of the Optimal Care Pathway
sections.content:
Optimal Care Pathways (OCPs) outline nationally agreed best practice across the entire cancer continuum. While the pathway steps are numbered in sequence, this does not mean the OCPs have to be used in a linear way. Optimal care for an individual is shaped by their cancer type, stage of disease and a range of personal characteristics and circumstances.

Supportive care is a critical pathway-spanning step for the individual and their families and carers.

This Optimal Care Pathway (OCP) provides guidance for the care of [population group] with cancer, from prevention and early detection through to survivorship or end-of-life. It is designed to be used alongside the relevant cancer-specific OCP to tailor care to the individual.

The OCP applies to [population group], defined for the purposes of this pathway as [insert how this population group is defined e.g. age range, characteristics or circumstances].

This pathway does not address [insert anything explicitly out of scope for this population group, e.g. specific settings, conditions or age boundaries].

This OCP should be considered together with relevant cancer-specific and other relevant population-based OCP(s) if required to create a tailored pathway that meets the needs of the individual.

sections.headingText: Genetic testing for inherited (germline) cancer risk
sections.headingPrinted: 1.1.3 Genetic testing for inherited (germline) cancer risk
sections.content:
15

Some cancers are caused or substantially influenced by inherited genetic variants. Identifying people with an elevated familial or genetic risk enables targeted surveillance and, in some cases, risk-reducing interventions. In addition to testing the individual, cascade testing can enhance the benefits of genetic testing by empowering family members to undertake surveillance and risk-reducing interventions.

Predictive genetic testing should be considered in individuals with:

•

a known pathogenic variant identified in their family

•

16

a significant family history of cancer, where genetic testing of previously affected family members has not been possible.

Predictive genetic testing may be coordinated by a clinical genetics service or familial cancer service. It requires specific consent and genetic counselling before and after the test. Cancer services should have clear referral pathways to genetics / familial cancer services.

Communication checklist when discussing cancer risk and early detection

✓ Provide information about risk and behaviour change in a non-judgemental way

– do not contact family members directly without the person’s consent

sections.content:
Following identification of concerning symptoms, or combinations of symptoms, signs and test results, the general practitioner (GP) should undertake appropriate clinical assessment and initial investigations to determine whether urgent or non-urgent referral to a cancer specialist is warranted. Investigation and referral decisions should be tailored to the person’s individual health status and social and cultural needs.

Assessment findings, and the decision-making process, should be clearly documented.

All patients should be provided with safety netting advice, including a planned timeframe for follow-up that is agreed with the patient, and the need for patient-initiated follow-up if new symptoms develop, if symptoms persist or worsen, or if the patient has further concerns.

When making a referral to investigate signs or symptoms of cancer in [population group], it is important to consider and / or include information about:

There are no specific considerations or inclusions when making a referral for investigation of signs or symptoms of cancer in [population group].

17

Considerations when making a referral

• Referrals do not need to be to a named cancer specialist. People can choose where to present the referral. People should be empowered to make an informed choice about their specialist.

• Referrals should take account of the person’s preference and ability to access public or private healthcare and ability to travel.

• Support informed decision making by encouraging the person to ask the cancer specialist about likely costs, waiting periods, and location for further tests and investigations.

• Referrals should contain all relevant clinical information about the patient’s condition for investigation, opinion, treatment and management.

• If access is via online referral, a lack of a hard copy should not delay referral.

• Where the referrer is not the person’s GP, prompt written communication should be sent to the person’s GP about the consultation.

• GPs retain responsibility for the person after referral to a cancer specialist. The GP (or referrer) should be notified if the person does not attend their appointment.

Essential inclusions when referring for suspected or diagnosed cancer

✓

Important psychosocial history and relevant medical history

✓

Family history, current symptoms, medications and allergies

✓

Results of current clinical investigations (e.g. imaging and pathology reports)

✓

Results of all prior relevant investigations

✓

Notification if an interpreter service is required.

Anyone diagnosed with cancer should have a detailed personal and family cancer history taken, covering at least three generations where possible. People with a strong family history of cancer may be referred to a familial cancer clinic to determine whether there is an inherited predisposition to cancer. Certain pathological subtypes of cancer, immunohistochemistry or tumour genetic tests may suggest an underlying inherited cancer predisposition.

Finding a germline mutation will have implications for the family. In families with a hereditary cancer predisposition, cascade testing allows for risk-reducing interventions and customised surveillance for those who carry the cancer predisposition genetic variant, thereby facilitating early detection, and resulting in better outcomes.

Treatment planning should be undertaken by a multidisciplinary team. The multidisciplinary team should meet to discuss newly diagnosed patients and recommend a treatment plan. Treatment planning should consider the intent of treatment (curative, control or palliation) and treatment goals, taking account of stage of disease and other factors.

25

Multidisciplinary input should be considered for all patients with cancer. However, not all cases may ultimately necessitate team discussion. In such cases, the team should apply agreed treatment protocols. Any people whose cases are not discussed at a multidisciplinary team meeting should at minimum be named on the agenda for noting.

Treatment planning discussions should include consideration of suitable clinical trials or research.

Multidisciplinary team membership should reflect both clinical and supportive care aspects of care. Pathology and radiology expertise are essential. Additional expertise or specialist services may be required for some patients.

A person’s GP contributes valuable information to treatment planning. They have knowledge of the person’s psychosocial history, comorbidities, medications, access to family and carer support, and locally available support services.

If someone does not have a regular GP, they should be encouraged and supported to find one.

Supportive care considerations during diagnosis and treatment planning , ,

• Receiving a cancer diagnosis can be a cause of significant psychological distress for the person, their families and carers. Early and proactive identification of supportive care needs is essential.

• A diagnosis of cancer can cause or exacerbate anxiety, depression, adjustment difficulties, treatment phobias, existential concerns, and interpersonal or psychosexual issues.

• Supportive care needs are personal to the individual and influenced by stage of disease, stage of life, gender, relationships, culture and other factors.

• Support to help people navigate the process of diagnosis and treatment planning is important.

• Consideration of family support where the person is a primary caregiver can reduce anxiety and improve acceptability of treatment.

29

• Prehabilitation before treatment may be appropriate to improve physical and psychological outcomes.

30

• For people of childbearing age, discussions about fertility preservation before the start of treatment are essential.

• Existential and spiritual concerns commonly emerge at diagnosis and during treatment planning.

31

• For people with advanced cancer, early referral to palliative care can improve outcomes.

Communication considerations during diagnosis and treatment planning

Communication about the multidisciplinary team

• It is important for people to understand the role of the multidisciplinary team and their ongoing role in treatment and care.

• Consent must be obtained before presenting the person’s case at a multidisciplinary meeting.

• The GP is a key member of the team. If the person does not have a regular GP, they should be actively encouraged to establish one.

Communicating a diagnosis of cancer

• Communication of a person’s diagnosis, prognosis (if the person wishes to know) and treatment options should be clear, compassionate and at a pace appropriate to the person.

Communicating the treatment plan

• A written treatment plan should include details of the treating team, contact details and instructions on when to call the hospital.

It is important to consider palliative from the point of diagnosis of advanced (metastatic) cancer. For people with advanced cancer, early integration of palliative care improves symptom management and quality of life, and in some cases is associated with survival benefits. , ,

It is essential for services to maintain clear pathways for early referral to palliative care and pain management, particularly if the multidisciplinary team does not include core membership of palliative care.

Key actions for introduction of palliative care

✓

Initiate early referral to palliative care services based on need and potential for benefit, not prognosis.

✓

Emphasise the value of palliative care in improving symptom management and quality of life.

✓

Reassess palliative care needs at each key clinical decision point.

✓

35

Ensure that carers and families receive information, support and guidance about their role in palliative care.

✓

Support the person and their family or carers to initiate advance care planning.

Complementary therapies may be used alongside conventional cancer treatments to support quality of life, wellbeing and symptom management. While some complementary therapies are supported by evidence, others are not. Integrative oncology combines evidence-based complementary therapies with conventional cancer care to address the physical, psychological and social impacts of cancer.

40

A person’s decision to use complementary therapies should not affect their access to or the quality of care they receive.

41

Key actions in relation to complementary therapies

✓

Proactively identify and document a person’s current or planned use of complementary therapies.

✓

42

Assess each therapy for safety, efficacy and to identify any potential toxicity or drug interaction.

✓

Communicate openly and without judgement when exploring the person’s reasons for wanting to use complementary therapies.

✓

Consider both the evidence of benefit and the costs of therapies during discussions.

✓

43

Where appropriate, discuss evidence-based integrative oncology approaches that may support symptom management, wellbeing and quality of life, such as physical activity, mindfulness-based interventions, yoga, acupuncture or oncology massage.

✓

If a person expresses interest in using complementary therapies, consider referral to a multidisciplinary team member with relevant expertise (e.g. a clinical pharmacist, dietitian or psychologist) to help them reach an informed decision.

sections.headingPrinted: 4.6 Involvement of the general practitioner in treatment for cancer
sections.content:
44

Early and sustained involvement of the person’s general practitioner (GP) during active treatment improves outcomes post-treatment. The role of the GP during treatment may include support for symptom management, management of co-morbidities, emotional and psychosocial support and referral to local services.

The GP can act as a consistent support for people and their families between specialist appointments.

A person’s GP should receive regular, timely communication throughout treatment, not only at the end of treatment.

Key actions for communicating with the GP during treatment

✓

Two-way communication should cover:

•

treatment plan, treatment intent (curative intent, control, palliation) and potential side effects

•

changes to treatment or medications

•

supportive and palliative care requirements

•

the patient's prognosis and their understanding of it

•

clinical trial enrolment

•

the presence of an advance care directive or substitute decision-maker

•

multidisciplinary team meeting recommendations.

✓

Consider use of a Chronic Condition Management Plan (GPCCMP) (can be billed as an MBS item)

Supportive care considerations during treatment , ,

• It is important to screen for supportive care needs at the start of treatment and when the intent of treatment changes. A person’s needs can shift significantly during active treatment.

• Family members and carers may also have supportive care needs.

• People may have needs across all five domains of supportive care during treatment.

• Support to help people navigate through their treatment pathway is important.

• Common supportive care needs for people with cancer are listed in the Supportive care principle <hyperlink to be added>

• Supportive care needs during treatment specific to [population group] include:

49

Rehabilitation ,

• People undergoing cancer treatment may experience a range of symptoms and side effects that affect their mobility and functional status which in turn influences activities of daily living and capacity for work.

• Referrals to services such as occupational therapy, speech pathology, dietetics, physiotherapy, exercise physiology, social work and psychology are important to assist with rehabilitation.

50

51

52

• Exercise is a safe and effective intervention throughout active cancer treatment and should be embedded as standard practice, not added as a supplement. , ,

• Exercise must be individually prescribed and delivered by an accredited exercise physiologist or physiotherapist with cancer care experience, tailored to the patient's current capacity, with a goal of transitioning to ongoing self-managed exercise.

• People who are living away from home for treatment are at particular risk of social isolation.

• Financial hardship is common during treatment due to loss of income, reduced work capacity and out-of-pocket treatment costs.

• People may need advice and support for legal considerations such as wills, care of dependents, and insurance, superannuation or social security claims on the basis of illness or disability.

sections.headingText: Care after initial treatment and recovery
sections.headingPrinted: Step 5: Care after initial treatment and recovery
sections.content:
Best practice guidance for supporting health and wellbeing following completion of active treatment for cancer, including follow-up care.

This step focuses on post-treatment care and recovery after treatment with curative intent. See Step 6 for guidance on supporting health and wellbeing for people living with advanced (metastatic) cancer.

The transition to post-treatment care is critical to long-term health. Some people need ongoing, hospital-based care. For others, a shared follow-up care arrangement with a general practitioner (GP) or nurse may be appropriate. This will vary depending on the type and stage of cancer and needs to be planned.

53

54

Models of follow-up care following completion of active treatment: ,

• Specialist-led care (hospital-based)

• Shared care (specialist and GP)

• GP-led or primary care-led

55

• Nurse-led models

Follow-up care may be supported by telehealth.

The appropriate model of follow-up care depends on cancer type, stage, predicted risk and the patient's individual clinical and psychosocial needs. Promoting self-management of emotional, psychosocial, physical, and functional impacts of cancer and its treatment is integral to follow-up care.

Key actions at the end of active treatment

✓

–

NCCN Distress Thermometer

complete a needs assessment using a validated tool such as the and document results

–

activate referral pathways to psychology, social work or counselling as required

–

prepare and deliver a treatment summary

–

develop a survivorship care plan in partnership with the patient

–

agree and clearly document the follow-up model of care with the lead clinician, GP and relevant multidisciplinary team members

–

ensure the patient understands the rapid re-entry pathway and the specific symptoms of recurrence to report.

At the end of initial treatment, a designated member of the multidisciplinary team should meet with the patient to:

✓

Provide copies of the treatment summary and survivorship care plan to the patient, their carer (if appropriate) and the person’s GP.

✓

Consider opportunities to participate in clinical trials or research related to survivorship care and long-term health and wellbeing.

See also

Research and clinical trials (Principle) <hyperlink to be added>

Physical considerations

Common long-term physical effects of treatment for cancer may include:

• cardiovascular toxicity

• endocrine effects

• neuropathy

• sexual dysfunction

• infertility

• cognitive changes

• fatigue

• impaired cardiac or pulmonary function

• risk of second malignancies.

Long-term physical effects of cancer that require particular focus in <population group> include:

Psychological considerations

• Fear of cancer recurrence (FCR) is the most commonly reported unmet need for people following completion of active treatment. People experience high levels of uncertainty about the future and fear of relapse.

– anxiety

– depression

– adjustment difficulties

– sleep disturbance.

• Other common psychological considerations for cancer include:

56

57

• Changes to sexual function, body image, fertility and intimate relationships are common survivorship concerns and are consistently under-assessed and underdiscussed. ,

58

• Carers also frequently experience distress, grief, and adjustment challenges during and after the person’s treatment.

Long-term psychological impacts of cancer that require particular focus in <population group> include:

Social considerations

59

60

• Financial hardship is common and often persists long after treatment. ,

• People may need support with insurance claims, superannuation, social security entitlements, legal matters such as wills or care of dependent children, and advance care planning.

Long-term social impacts of cancer that require particular focus in <population group> include:

A comprehensive survivorship care plan extends beyond medical follow-up to support overall wellness. It should be grounded in an understanding of the person’s cancer and treatments and should support self-management as well as providing information and referrals to relevant sources of support as appropriate. Uploading of the plan to My Health Record can support implementation, coordination and ongoing monitoring.

Key inclusions in a survivorship / wellness plan

Physical activity

✓

Recommendations for exercise tailored to the patient's capacity, treatment history and goals

✓

Referral to physiotherapist or exercise physiologist where indicated

Nutrition

✓

Recommendations for diet and nutrition

✓

Referral to dietitian where nutritional needs are complex or treatment has affected eating

Wellbeing and risk reduction

✓

Recommendations for ongoing wellbeing and to reduce risk of recurrence:

•

maintaining a healthy body weight

•

smoking or vaping cessation

•

reduce or avoid alcohol

•

sun smart behaviours

Mental health and wellbeing

✓

Screen for fear of cancer recurrence, anxiety, depression and cognitive changes at follow-up appointments

✓

Consider developing a mental health plan if required

✓

Refer to psychology, social work or peer support as indicated

Practical and financial wellbeing

✓

Identify financial hardship, return to work/study concerns and carer impacts early

✓

Connect patients to financial counselling, social work and relevant support services

Fertility counselling

✓

Recommendations for ongoing contraception needs (noting that some treatments require contraception for a defined period post-treatment)

✓

Referral to a fertility specialist for people of reproductive age who wish to conceive

• Fear of cancer recurrence (FCR) is the most commonly reported unmet need among cancer survivors. It should be routinely assessed at follow-up appointments, not assumed to diminish over time. ,

• Anxiety, depression, cognitive changes, sleep disturbance and adjustment difficulties are common in survivorship.

65

• Carers frequently experience their own distress, grief, and adjustment challenges during and after the patient's treatment.

• People can face unique challenges with financial hardship, return to work or study, ongoing care costs and legal matters.

• Changes to sexual function, body image, fertility and intimate relationships are common survivorship concerns and are consistently under-assessed and underdiscussed. ,

• People need information, tools and support to manage their health after initial treatment, including how to monitor for symptoms of recurrence, when to seek urgent review, how to access services, and how to maintain the wellness behaviours outlined in their survivorship care plan.

sections.headingText: Managing residual, recurrent or metastatic disease
sections.headingPrinted: Step 6: Managing residual, recurrent or metastatic disease
sections.content: Best practice guidance for management of residual, recurrent or metastatic disease. Includes guidance about palliative care and advance care planning and about supporting health and wellbeing for people living with advanced (metastatic) cancer.

sections.headingText: Detecting residual, recurrent or metastatic disease
sections.headingPrinted: 6.1 Detecting residual, recurrent or metastatic disease
sections.content:
Residual, recurrent and metastatic cancer are clinically distinct states. They may be detected through:

•

routine surveillance: detected on scheduled imaging, blood tests or clinical review during the post-treatment follow-up period

•

incidental finding: detected during investigation for an unrelated condition.

•

patient-reported symptoms: which may be new or worsening, at or between scheduled appointments.

Signs and symptoms will depend on the location of residual, recurrent or metastatic disease.

Population-specific factors influencing detection of residual, recurrent or metastatic cancer

Detection of residual, recurrent or metastatic disease in [population group] may be influenced by factors such as:

•

Detection of signs and symptoms of recurrent, residual or metastatic cancer in [population group] are similar to those described for initial presentation. See Step 2 for details.

sections.headingText: Advanced disease states and treatment intent
sections.headingPrinted: 6.3.1 Advanced disease states and treatment intent
sections.content: Understanding and communicating the disease state and treatment intent is essential for treatment planning. Treatment intent may change from symptom control to palliation as the disease evolves. Treatment intent and goals of care should be discussed with the person and their family / carer at each key decision point and documented in the medical record.

sections.headingText: Treatment planning and the multidisciplinary team
sections.headingPrinted: 6.3.2 Treatment planning and the multidisciplinary team
sections.content:
All patients with confirmed or suspected residual, recurrent or metastatic disease must be reviewed by a multidisciplinary team. The complexity of advanced disease requires input from multiple specialties to ensure all treatment options are considered. The multidisciplinary team for advanced or metastatic cancer may include additional / different members from the team involved in developing the initial treatment plan.

sections.headingText: Supporting health and wellbeing for people with advanced (metastatic) cancer
sections.headingPrinted: 6.5 Supporting health and wellbeing for people with advanced (metastatic) cancer
sections.content:
71

72

Improvements in cancer surveillance, diagnostics, and treatment mean that people with advanced (metastatic) cancer are living for long periods with disease control. A focus on survivorship care is as essential for people with advanced cancer as it is for people with earlier stage disease. COSA-endorsed MASCC-ASCO Standards and Practice Recommendations highlight the importance of prioritising and providing quality and consistent survivorship care for people affected by advanced (metastatic) cancer from the point of diagnosis.

73

Considerations for health and wellbeing highlighted in Step 5 are relevant following a diagnosis of advanced or metastatic disease. However, contributing factors may be different, and the frequency and intensity of needs may vary.

74

Physical needs for people with advanced (metastatic) cancer

Common physical needs include:

• managing pain

• maintaining independence

• preserving physical function

• fatigue and lack of energy

• adapting to life roles and daily activities

• managing side effects or complications

Physical needs specific to [population group] with advanced (metastatic) cancer include:

75

Psychological needs for people with advanced (metastatic) cancer

Common psychological needs include:

• uncertainty

• fear of cancer progression

• fear of physical deterioration and pain

• depression and anxiety

• stress and worry

Psychological needs specific to [population group] with advanced (metastatic) cancer include:

76

Social considerations for people with advanced (metastatic) cancer

Common social / financial needs include:

• loss of income

• extra expenditure

• financial planning

• assistance with insurance

• accessing social services

Social needs specific to [population group] with advanced (metastatic) cancer include:

Palliative care is a core component of managing residual, recurrent and metastatic cancer. Palliative care services are provided by a range of health professionals. Involvement of different health professionals should be considered based on individual needs of the person receiving care.

79

Access to palliative care may be enabled by telehealth. ,

80

Referral for palliative care support should be based on a person’s need rather than prognosis.

Advance care planning is important for all patients with a cancer diagnosis but especially those with advanced disease.

Patients should be encouraged to think and talk about their healthcare values and preferences with family or carers, appoint a substitute decision-maker and consider developing an advance care directive to convey their preferences for future health care in the event they become unable to communicate their wishes.

The person’s general practitioner (GP) plays an important role in symptom management, management of comorbidities, psychosocial support and referral to local and community-based services. For some people, the GP may be the primary provider of palliative care.

A diagnosis of advanced disease, and any change in treatment intent, should be communicated to the GP promptly so that care remains coordinated.

As palliative care is introduced, the GP is well placed to work alongside the palliative care team and other specialists and to support the person and their family with advance care planning. The GP's role in symptom management, comorbidity care, mental health and local referral should be actively supported and clearly communicated.

Key actions for communication with the GP in relation to residual, recurrent or metastatic disease

✓

–

the treatment plan and intent

–

changes to treatment

–

supportive and palliative care needs

–

prognosis

–

any advance care directive or substitute decision-maker

–

shared care arrangements.

Find out more

Information about developing a GP Chronic Condition Management Plan

Supportive care considerations for people with residual, recurrent or metastatic disease

• A new diagnosis of advanced disease is a significant event for patients and carers. Common unmet needs for people with advanced (metastatic) cancer are listed in section 6.5. <hyperlink to be added>

• Recurrent, residual or metastatic disease often brings fear of death and dying, existential distress and anticipatory grief.

• Declining mobility and functional status are common with recurrent disease.

• Cognitive changes from treatment or disease progression can affect memory, attention and concentration.

• A substitute decision-maker and an advance care plan / directive can be vital to ensure a person’s wishes are addressed at this time.

82

• Loss of income and extra expenditure on treatment and care can cause financial hardship. People may need financial planning advice or assistance with access to superannuation, insurance or social services.

• Support with legal matters such as wills, care of dependent children, and terminal-illness or permanent-disability claims may be needed.

• Carers and family members need their own assessment and support, including respite.

sections.content: Best practice guidance for maintaining quality of life and meeting health and supportive care needs as people with cancer approach the end of life. Includes guidance for supporting family and carers.

End-of-life care focuses on maintaining quality of life, managing symptoms, supporting a person’s values and preferences, and meeting the needs of families and carers. Safe and high-quality end-of-life care should be:

•

person-centred and include family and carers

•

align with values, needs and wishes

•

consider cultural, spiritual and psychosocial needs

•

83

not offer unreasonable hope.

84

The first step in providing safe and high-quality end-of-life care is to recognise people who would benefit from such care.

Key clinical triggers indicating end-of-life care is appropriate

• Functional status declining despite optimal management (ECOG performance status 3–4 or equivalent)

• Weight loss, reduced oral intake, increasing fatigue, reduced mobility

• Increasing symptom burden not adequately controlled

• Frequent hospital admissions or presentations

• Person or family expressing awareness that death is approaching

Find out more

Resources about end-of-life care

The multidisciplinary team for end-of-life care should include:

•

Palliative medicine specialist

•

Specialist palliative care nurse / clinical nurse practitioner

•

General practitioner (GP) (with engagement and communication throughout)

•

Pain specialist

•

Clinical psychologist

•

Social worker

•

Pastoral or spiritual care worker

•

Bereavement counsellor

•

Cultural liaison officer or cultural expert

•

Music therapist or art therapist

•

Allied health (physiotherapy, occupational therapy, dietetics as relevant)

•

CanTeen for children of parents with cancer.

The end-of-life care team for [population group] should include:

•

End-of-life care planning checklist

✓

Ensure the person has an advance care directive in place

✓

Ensure the person has been referred to palliative care

✓

Discuss and document the person’s preferred place of care and death

✓

Consider referral to home and community-based care, specialist community palliative care workers or community nursing as appropriate

✓

Respond to any questions or information requests for voluntary assisted dying

End-of-life care setting checklist

✓ Ensure the transition to the chosen care setting is planned, not reactive

✓ Offer access to private physical spaces for gatherings as required

✓ Coordinate with home-based community palliative care services, residential hospice, or inpatient palliative unit as appropriate

Comprehensive symptom management is the core clinical work of end-of-life care.

85

Timely identification and management of palliative care emergencies is important for symptom management and to maintain quality of life.

Assess and actively manage the following:

Pain

pain assessment tools

Use validated and ensure regular analgesia review; refer to pain specialist if needed

Breathlessness

Optimise pharmacological and non-pharmacological management

Other physical symptoms

Assess for and manage nausea and vomiting, fatigue and weakness, mouth care and skin integrity

Anxiety and psychological distress

Screen regularly and refer to psychology or psychiatric services

Delirium

Identify and manage reversible causes; provide family support

Nutritional decline and eating difficulties

Involve a dietitian, discuss with patient and family

Carers and family members should receive support through the end-of-life period and in bereavement.

Key actions to support families and carers

✓ Undertake a specific needs assessment for families and carers and re-evaluate it regularly.

✓ Ensure families and carers receive information, support and guidance about their caring role according to their needs and wishes, including practical guidance on day-to-day care and medications where care is provided at home.

✓ Assess for anticipatory grief and the risk of prolonged grief, and refer to psychological, social work, pastoral or bereavement support as required.

✓ Provide information about practical matters, including available support services, financial and legal considerations, and what to do after a death, and offer referral to bereavement support that continues after the person has died.

✓ Actions to support families and carers of [population group] at end of life include:

The GP often has a central role in end-of-life care, particularly when a person chooses to be cared for, and to die, at home.

Working alongside the specialist and community palliative care teams, the GP can:

•

provide and coordinate symptom management

•

attend the person in the community

•

offer continuity of care for the person

•

provides ongoing support to the family and carers, including into bereavement.

The GP should be kept fully informed and involved in major developments in the person’s care. Clear communication about the person’s condition, goals of care and preferred place of care and death supports a planned rather than reactive approach.

Key actions for communicating with the GP regarding end-of-life care

✓

Keep the GP fully informed of major developments and involve them in end-of-life care planning

✓

End-of-life care planning should be discussed with the GP so that the person’s needs and goals can be met in their preferred environment.

sections.content:
Voluntary Assisted Dying (VAD) is legally available in all Australian states and the Australian Capital Territory (ACT). There are legal requirements all medical practitioners must comply with, irrespective of personal views.

All states except Tasmania and the ACT require the medical condition to be progressive. In all states and the ACT, clinicians who have not completed mandatory VAD training must decline requests. Clinicians who are unable to provide VAD services should comply with the legal requirements in their jurisdiction, including providing information about appropriate referral pathways where required.

Clinicians may make a conscientious objection to participating in a VAD process but must be aware of their jurisdiction-specific obligations, which vary in terms of information provision and referral requirements.

VAD care navigators exist in all states and the ACT. Refer patients and families to these services for information and support.

Find out more

Resources about voluntary assisted dying

Supportive care considerations at end-of-life

• Emotional and psychological distress is common, including anticipatory grief, fear of death or dying, anxiety, depression and interpersonal difficulties.

• Physical symptoms and a decline in mobility or functional status are common and may affect the person’s care needs and place of care.

• People may need support to appoint a substitute decision-maker and complete an advance care directive, and to manage legal and financial matters such as making a will, arranging care of dependent children, and lodging insurance, superannuation or Centrelink claims on the basis of terminal illness or permanent disability.

• Families and carers have their own needs, including practical support, respite and spiritual support.

• Cultural, spiritual and religious beliefs and practices strongly shape what matters most to a person and their family at the end of life and should be respected and accommodated.

• Supportive care considerations at end of life for [population group] include:

Supportive care checklist

✓ Assess physical, psychological, social, spiritual and existential needs using a validated tool and document the results, reassessing as needs change

✓ Assess and actively manage symptoms, and refer to specialist palliative care, pain and allied health services as required

✓ Confirm the person has an advance care directive and substitute decision-maker in place

✓ Discuss and document the person’s preferred place of care and place of death

✓ Identify and support practical, legal and financial needs, including a will, care of dependent children and insurance, superannuation or Centrelink claims

✓ Assess carer and family needs and offer support, respite and referral, including for anticipatory grief, bereavement and support for dependent children

This template has been created to help developers of population-based Optimal Care Pathways (OCPs) develop a high-quality and evidence-based resource that is consistent with the library of existing pathways. The template mirrors the core content of the cancer-specific OCP template and provides space to add considerations for a particular population group relevant to the Principles for Optimal Cancer Care <hyperlink to be added> and each pathway step. It contains two types of content:
• core content that is standard across all OCPs and cannot be changed
• editable content that must be completed or adapted for your population group.
OCPs@canceraustralia.gov.au
• Follow these instructions when developing your OCP. If you have any questions, contact Cancer Australia at
• Keep content high level and scannable. Avoid lengthy narrative paragraphs.
• Review the Principles for Optimal Cancer Care <hyperlink to be added> when developing content to avoid duplication and identify where cross-referencing is appropriate.
• Black text is core content that cannot be edited. This is standard content across all OCPs.
• Text [highlighted in yellow] indicates words to be added / adapted for this population group / OCP.
• Purple boxes indicate content requiring developer input specific to this population group / OCP. Instructions are provided in purple text.

• Key considerations tables contain brief statements summarising what optimal care looks like at each step of the cancer pathway. Follow the purple prompts to add population-specific considerations as new rows in these tables.
• Checklists are actionable items for health professionals at key decision points. Follow the purple prompts to add any population-specific actions as new rows in these lists.
• Supportive care sections: Each step includes supportive care considerations. Follow the purple prompts to add population-specific content.

• 'Find out more' boxes are curated links to guidelines and resources. These will appear on the digital hub with links from relevant sections. Follow the purple prompts to add any specific resources for this population group and include the associated hyperlink.
• Numbered headings and subheadings cannot be changed or reordered. This ensures consistency across the OCP library and aids with digitisation.
• Additional third-level subheadings (i.e. non-numbered headings) can be added within sections. Consider additional sub-headings sparingly.
• Sections can be removed where content is not relevant to this population group.

If you identify content that you believe should be added as core information to the template (e.g. a new section, consideration or action relevant to all population-based OCPs), note this separately with Cancer Australia. Developers cannot edit core template content directly. Suggestions will be considered as part of the centralised review process.

Optimal Care Pathways (OCPs) are nationally endorsed evidence-and consensus-based guides to best practice care across the cancer continuum. They set a national standard for consistent, high-quality cancer care for everyone in Australia, regardless of who they are or where they live.

OCPs are embedded within the as national standards for delivery of high-quality, consistent cancer care. Their development is guided by the , which provides a consistent approach to prioritisation, development, update and endorsement of OCPs and supports their adoption into health systems.
Map nationally agreed best practice approaches to cancer care, placing the person with cancer at the centre of care.
Set the standard for quality cancer care in Australia by describing what optimal care looks like across the cancer continuum.
Reduce unwarranted variation in access, care and outcomes by providing a nationally consistent approach to benchmark and improve services and practice.
Guide service improvement by helping health services identify gaps and opportunities to achieve optimal care.
Support clinician practice by giving health professionals evidence-based information, checklists and tools to understand and deliver best practice care.
Inform and empower people affected by cancer to have informed conversations with their healthcare teams about optimal care and what they should expect.
Drive equity by promoting accessible, culturally safe and responsive care that reduces unwarranted variations in access, care and outcomes.

The Principles for Optimal Cancer Care set the foundations for delivery of information, care and support for everyone who is at risk of and affected by cancer. Everyone in the healthcare system is responsible for delivering cancer care aligned to the Principles.
Principles are relevant to all cancer types and all populations. Population-based OCPs may identify unique considerations for implementation for a particular population group.
Equity <Link to Principle > <hyperlink to be added>
Health equity in cancer outcomes is the absence of disparities for people with different levels of social advantage.
Person-centred care <Link to Principle > <hyperlink to be added>
Person-centred care means informing and involving people in their care, and respecting and responding to their individual needs, preferences and values, as well as those of their families and carers.
Safe and quality care <Link to Principle> <hyperlink to be added>
Safe and quality care means delivering the most appropriate and best-value care, while keeping people safe from preventable harm in the delivery of that care.
Multidisciplinary care <Link to Principle> <hyperlink to be added>

Multidisciplinary care is an integrated team approach that involves all relevant health professionals discussing all relevant treatment options and making joint recommendations about treatment and supportive care plans that consider the individual characteristics and preferences of the person with cancer.
Supportive care <Link to Principle> <hyperlink to be added>

Supportive care involves prevention and management of the adverse effects of cancer and its treatment, including management of physical and psychological symptoms and side effects across the cancer continuum. Supportive care aims to improve the quality of rehabilitation, secondary cancer prevention, survivorship, and end-of-life care.
Navigation and care coordination <Link to Principle> <hyperlink to be added>

Navigation and care coordination are related person-centred interventions that aim to empower patients, families and carers affected by cancer to facilitate safe and timely access to optimal cancer-related care and support.
Communication <Link to Principle> <hyperlink to be added>
Good communication is an essential part of cancer care and a responsibility of everyone involved in health care across the cancer continuum.
Research and clinical trials <Link to Principle> <hyperlink to be added>

Research and clinical trials generate evidence to improve understanding of cancer and to accelerate progress in prevention, detection, diagnosis, treatment, supportive care, survivorship care, palliative and end-of-life care.

Some cancers are caused or substantially influenced by inherited genetic variants. Identifying people with an elevated familial or genetic risk enables targeted surveillance and, in some cases, risk-reducing interventions. In addition to testing the individual, cascade testing can enhance the benefits of genetic testing by empowering family members to undertake surveillance and risk-reducing interventions.
Predictive genetic testing should be considered in individuals with:
a known pathogenic variant identified in their family
a significant family history of cancer, where genetic testing of previously affected family members has not been possible.

Predictive genetic testing may be coordinated by a clinical genetics service or familial cancer service. It requires specific consent and genetic counselling before and after the test. Cancer services should have clear referral pathways to genetics / familial cancer services.

Following identification of concerning symptoms, or combinations of symptoms, signs and test results, the general practitioner (GP) should undertake appropriate clinical assessment and initial investigations to determine whether urgent or non-urgent referral to a cancer specialist is warranted. Investigation and referral decisions should be tailored to the person’s individual health status and social and cultural needs.
Assessment findings, and the decision-making process, should be clearly documented.

All patients should be provided with safety netting advice, including a planned timeframe for follow-up that is agreed with the patient, and the need for patient-initiated follow-up if new symptoms develop, if symptoms persist or worsen, or if the patient has further concerns.

Considerations when making a referral
• Referrals do not need to be to a named cancer specialist. People can choose where to present the referral. People should be empowered to make an informed choice about their specialist.
• Referrals should take account of the person’s preference and ability to access public or private healthcare and ability to travel.
• Support informed decision making by encouraging the person to ask the cancer specialist about likely costs, waiting periods, and location for further tests and investigations.
• Referrals should contain all relevant clinical information about the patient’s condition for investigation, opinion, treatment and management.
• If access is via online referral, a lack of a hard copy should not delay referral.
• Where the referrer is not the person’s GP, prompt written communication should be sent to the person’s GP about the consultation.
• GPs retain responsibility for the person after referral to a cancer specialist. The GP (or referrer) should be notified if the person does not attend their appointment.
Essential inclusions when referring for suspected or diagnosed cancer
Important psychosocial history and relevant medical history
Family history, current symptoms, medications and allergies
Results of current clinical investigations (e.g. imaging and pathology reports)
Results of all prior relevant investigations
Notification if an interpreter service is required.

Embedding precision medicine diagnostics in routine cancer care can inform diagnostic and treatment decisions. Three distinct but complementary forms of genetic testing can be considered as part of the diagnostic work-up:
germline testing
somatic testing
pharmacogenetic testing.
Molecular tumour boards play an important role in the assessment of complex genomic findings.
Key actions for genetic and genomic testing
Discuss requirements for genetic or genomic testing at the multidisciplinary team meeting
Consider referral to a molecular tumour board (where appropriate and available)
Consider the impact of timeframes for genetic or genomic testing on timelines for starting treatment
Ensure effective oncology–pathology collaborations to enable timely genetic and genomic testing
Order genetic tests as clinically indicated and in accordance with current evidence and guidelines
Medicare funds some germline tests via the Medicare Benefits Schedule
Other tests may be funded through state health systems

Anyone diagnosed with cancer should have a detailed personal and family cancer history taken, covering at least three generations where possible. People with a strong family history of cancer may be referred to a familial cancer clinic to determine whether there is an inherited predisposition to cancer. Certain pathological subtypes of cancer, immunohistochemistry or tumour genetic tests may suggest an underlying inherited cancer predisposition.

Finding a germline mutation will have implications for the family. In families with a hereditary cancer predisposition, cascade testing allows for risk-reducing interventions and customised surveillance for those who carry the cancer predisposition genetic variant, thereby facilitating early detection, and resulting in better outcomes.

Treatment planning should be undertaken by a multidisciplinary team. The multidisciplinary team should meet to discuss newly diagnosed patients and recommend a treatment plan. Treatment planning should consider the intent of treatment (curative, control or palliation) and treatment goals, taking account of stage of disease and other factors.

Multidisciplinary input should be considered for all patients with cancer. However, not all cases may ultimately necessitate team discussion. Treatment planning discussions should include consideration of suitable clinical trials or research.

Multidisciplinary team membership should reflect both clinical and supportive care aspects of care. Pathology and radiology expertise are essential. Additional expertise or specialist services may be required for some patients.

Supportive care considerations during diagnosis and treatment planning , ,

• Receiving a cancer diagnosis can be a cause of significant psychological distress for the person, their families and carers. Early and proactive identification of supportive care needs is essential.
• A diagnosis of cancer can cause or exacerbate anxiety, depression, adjustment difficulties, treatment phobias, existential concerns, and interpersonal or psychosexual issues.
• Supportive care needs are personal to the individual and influenced by stage of disease, stage of life, gender, relationships, culture and other factors.
• Support to help people navigate the process of diagnosis and treatment planning is important.
• Consideration of family support where the person is a primary caregiver can reduce anxiety and improve acceptability of treatment.
• Prehabilitation before treatment may be appropriate to improve physical and psychological outcomes.
• For people of childbearing age, discussions about fertility preservation before the start of treatment are essential.
• Existential and spiritual concerns commonly emerge at diagnosis and during treatment planning.
• For people with advanced cancer, early referral to palliative care can improve outcomes.

Complementary therapies may be used alongside conventional cancer treatments to support quality of life, wellbeing and symptom management. While some complementary therapies are supported by evidence, others are not. Integrative oncology combines evidence-based complementary therapies with conventional cancer care to address the physical, psychological and social impacts of cancer.
A person’s decision to use complementary therapies should not affect their access to or the quality of care they receive.
<Optional> Complete the box
Key actions in relation to complementary therapies
Proactively identify and document a person’s current or planned use of complementary therapies.
Assess each therapy for safety, efficacy and to identify any potential toxicity or drug interaction.
Communicate openly and without judgement when exploring the person’s reasons for wanting to use complementary therapies.
Consider both the evidence of benefit and the costs of therapies during discussions.

Where appropriate, discuss evidence-based integrative oncology approaches that may support symptom management, wellbeing and quality of life, such as physical activity, mindfulness-based interventions, yoga, acupuncture or oncology massage.

If a person expresses interest in using complementary therapies, consider referral to a multidisciplinary team member with relevant expertise (e.g. a clinical pharmacist, dietitian or psychologist) to help them reach an informed decision.

Best practice guidance for supporting health and wellbeing following completion of active treatment for cancer, including follow-up care.

This step focuses on post-treatment care and recovery after treatment with curative intent. See Step 6 for guidance on supporting health and wellbeing for people living with advanced (metastatic) cancer.

The transition to post-treatment care is critical to long-term health. Some people need ongoing, hospital-based care. For others, a shared follow-up care arrangement with a general practitioner (GP) or nurse may be appropriate. This will vary depending on the type and stage of cancer and needs to be planned.
Models of follow-up care following completion of active treatment: ,
• Specialist-led care (hospital-based)

Best practice guidance for management of residual, recurrent or metastatic disease. Includes guidance about palliative care and advance care planning and about supporting health and wellbeing for people living with advanced (metastatic) cancer.
Residual, recurrent and metastatic cancer are clinically distinct states. They may be detected through:
routine surveillance: detected on scheduled imaging, blood tests or clinical review during the post-treatment follow-up period
incidental finding: detected during investigation for an unrelated condition.
patient-reported symptoms: which may be new or worsening, at or between scheduled appointments.
Signs and symptoms will depend on the location of residual, recurrent or metastatic disease.

Understanding and communicating the disease state and treatment intent is essential for treatment planning. Treatment intent may change from symptom control to palliation as the disease evolves. Treatment intent and goals of care should be discussed with the person and their family / carer at each key decision point and documented in the medical record.

All patients with confirmed or suspected residual, recurrent or metastatic disease must be reviewed by a multidisciplinary team. The complexity of advanced disease requires input from multiple specialties to ensure all treatment options are considered. The multidisciplinary team for advanced or metastatic cancer may include additional / different members from the team involved in developing the initial treatment plan.

Supportive care considerations for people with residual, recurrent or metastatic disease

• A new diagnosis of advanced disease is a significant event for patients and carers. Common unmet needs for people with advanced (metastatic) cancer are listed in section 6.5. <hyperlink to be added>
• Recurrent, residual or metastatic disease often brings fear of death and dying, existential distress and anticipatory grief.

• A substitute decision-maker and an advance care plan / directive can be vital to ensure a person’s wishes are addressed at this time.

Best practice guidance for maintaining quality of life and meeting health and supportive care needs as people with cancer approach the end of life. Includes guidance for supporting family and carers.

End-of-life care focuses on maintaining quality of life, managing symptoms, supporting a person’s values and preferences, and meeting the needs of families and carers. Safe and high-quality end-of-life care should be:
person-centred and include family and carers
align with values, needs and wishes
consider cultural, spiritual and psychosocial needs
not offer unreasonable hope.
The first step in providing safe and high-quality end-of-life care is to recognise people who would benefit from such care.
Key clinical triggers indicating end-of-life care is appropriate
• Functional status declining despite optimal management (ECOG performance status 3–4 or equivalent)
• Weight loss, reduced oral intake, increasing fatigue, reduced mobility
• Increasing symptom burden not adequately controlled
• Frequent hospital admissions or presentations
• Person or family expressing awareness that death is approaching

Voluntary Assisted Dying (VAD) is legally available in all Australian states and the Australian Capital Territory (ACT). There are legal requirements all medical practitioners must comply with, irrespective of personal views.

All states except Tasmania and the ACT require the medical condition to be progressive. In all states and the ACT, clinicians who have not completed mandatory VAD training must decline requests. Clinicians who are unable to provide VAD services should comply with the legal requirements in their jurisdiction, including providing information about appropriate referral pathways where required.

Clinicians may make a conscientious objection to participating in a VAD process but must be aware of their jurisdiction-specific obligations, which vary in terms of information provision and referral requirements.
VAD care navigators exist in all states and the ACT. Refer patients and families to these services for information and support.

Supportive care considerations at end-of-life
• Emotional and psychological distress is common, including anticipatory grief, fear of death or dying, anxiety, depression and interpersonal difficulties.
• Physical symptoms and a decline in mobility or functional status are common and may affect the person’s care needs and place of care.

• People may need support to appoint a substitute decision-maker and complete an advance care directive, and to manage legal and financial matters such as making a will, arranging care of dependent children, and lodging insurance, superannuation or Centrelink claims on the basis of terminal illness or permanent disability.
• Families and carers have their own needs, including practical support, respite and spiritual support.
• Cultural, spiritual and religious beliefs and practices strongly shape what matters most to a person and their family at the end of life and should be respected and accommodated.
